text: There are five ways of attacking with fire. The first is to burn soldiers in their camp; the second is to burn stores; the third is to burn baggage trains; the fourth is to burn arsenals and magazines; the fifth is to hurl dropping fire amongst the enemy.
In order to carry out an attack, we must have means available. The material for raising fire should always be kept in readiness.
There is a proper season for making attacks with fire, and special days for starting a conflagration.

The proper season is when the weather is very dry; the special days are those when the moon is in the constellations of the Sieve, the Wall, the Wing or the Cross-bar; for these four are all days of rising wind.
In attacking with fire, one should be prepared to meet five possible developments.
When fire breaks out inside the enemy's camp, respond at once with an attack from without.
If there is an outbreak of fire, but the enemy's soldiers remain quiet, bide your time and do not attack.
When the force of the flames has reached its height, follow it up with an attack, if that is practicable; if not, stay where you are.
If it is possible to make an assault with fire from without, do not wait for it to break out within, but deliver your attack at a favorable moment.
When you start a fire, be to windward of it. Do not attack from the leeward.
A wind that rises in the daytime lasts long, but a night breeze soon falls.
In every army, the five developments connected with fire must be known, the movements of the stars calculated, and a watch kept for the proper days.
Those who use fire as an aid to the attack show intelligence; those who use water as an aid to the attack gain an accession of strength.
By means of water, an enemy may be intercepted, but not robbed of all his belongings.
Unhappy is the fate of one who tries to win his battles and succeed in his attacks without cultivating the spirit of enterprise; for the result is waste of time and general stagnation.
The enlightened ruler lays his plans well ahead; the good general cultivates his resources.
Move not unless you see an advantage; use not your troops unless there is something to be gained; fight not unless the position is critical.
No ruler should put troops into the field merely to gratify his own spleen; no general should fight a battle simply out of pique.
If it is to your advantage, make a forward move; if not, stay where you are. Anger may in time change to gladness; vexation may be succeeded by content.
A kingdom that has once been destroyed can never come again into being; nor can the dead ever be brought back to life. Hence the enlightened ruler is heedful and the good general full of caution.

Raising a host of a hundred thousand men and marching them great distances entails heavy loss on the people and a drain on the resources of the State. The daily expenditure will amount to a thousand ounces of silver.
There will be commotion at home and abroad, and men will drop down exhausted on the highways. As many as seven hundred thousand families will be impeded in their labor.
Hostile armies may face each other for years, striving for the victory which is decided in a single day.

To remain in ignorance of the enemy's condition simply because one grudges the outlay of a hundred ounces of silver in honors and emoluments, is the height of inhumanity. One who acts thus is no leader of men, no present help to his sovereign, no master of victory.

What enables the wise sovereign and the good general to strike and conquer, and achieve things beyond the reach of ordinary men, is foreknowledge. This foreknowledge cannot be elicited from spirits; it cannot be obtained inductively from experience, nor by any deductive calculation. Knowledge of the enemy's dispositions can only be obtained from other men.

Hence the use of spies, of whom there are five classes: local spies; inward spies; converted spies; doomed spies; surviving spies. When these five kinds of spy are all at work, none can discover the secret system. This is called divine manipulation of the threads. It is the sovereign's most precious faculty.

Having local spies means employing the services of the inhabitants of a district. Having inward spies, making use of officials of the enemy. Having converted spies, getting hold of the enemy's spies and using them for our own purposes. Having doomed spies, doing certain things openly for purposes of deception, and allowing our spies to know of them and report them to the enemy. Surviving spies, finally, are those who bring back news from the enemy's camp.

It is that which none in the whole army are more intimate relations to be maintained than with spies. None should be more liberally rewarded. In no other business should greater secrecy be preserved. Spies cannot be usefully employed without a certain intuitive sagacity. They cannot be properly managed without benevolence and straightforwardness. Without subtle ingenuity of mind, one cannot make certain of the truth of their reports.

Be subtle! be subtle! and use your spies for every kind of business. If a secret piece of news is divulged by a spy before the time is ripe, he must be put to death together with the man to whom the secret was told.

It is only the enlightened ruler and the wise general who will use the highest intelligence of the army for purposes of spying and thereby they achieve great results. Spies are a most important element in war, because on them depends an army's ability to move.
What are the nine varieties of ground? Dispersive, facile, contentious, open, intersecting highways, serious, difficult, hemmed-in, and desperate ground.
What is dispersive ground? Ground where a chieftain is fighting in his own territory.
What is facile ground? Ground where a chieftain has penetrated into hostile territory but to no great distance.
What is contentious ground? Ground whose possession imports great advantage to either side.
What is open ground? Ground on which each side has liberty of movement.
What is ground of intersecting highways? Ground which forms the key to three contiguous states, so that he who occupies it first has most of the Empire at his command.
What is serious ground? Ground where an army has penetrated into the heart of a hostile country, leaving fortified cities in its rear.
What is difficult ground? Mountain forests, rugged steeps, marshes and fens, all country hard to traverse.
What is hemmed-in ground? Ground reached through narrow gorges, from which we can only retire by tortuous paths, so that a small number of the enemy suffices to crush a large body of our men.
What is desperate ground? Ground on which we can only be saved from destruction by fighting without delay.
What should be done on dispersive, facile and contentious ground? Fight not on dispersive ground, halt not on facile ground, and attack not on contentious ground.
What should be done on open and intersecting-highway ground? Do not block the enemy's way on open ground, and join hands with allies on intersecting highways.
What should be done on serious and difficult ground? Gather in plunder on serious ground, and keep steadily on the march in difficult ground.
What should be done on hemmed-in and desperate ground? Resort to stratagem on hemmed-in ground, and fight on desperate ground.

What did skillful leaders of old know how to do? Drive a wedge between the enemy's front and rear, prevent co-operation between his large and small divisions, and hinder good troops from rescuing bad and officers from rallying their men.

What did skillful leaders do when the enemy's men were united, or when advantage favored them? They kept the enemy in disorder when united, and made a forward move when it was to their advantage, stopping still otherwise.
How should one cope with a great host in orderly array on the point of attacking? Begin by seizing something the opponent holds dear; then he will be amenable to your will.
What is the essence of war? Rapidity: take advantage of the enemy's unreadiness, make your way by unexpected routes, and attack unguarded spots.
What is the principle for an invading force regarding penetration? The further you penetrate into a country, the greater the solidarity of your troops, and the defenders will not prevail against you.
How should an invading army be supplied? Make forays in fertile country to supply the army with food.
How should an invading commander care for his men? Study their well-being, do not overtax them, concentrate energy, hoard strength, keep the army moving, and devise unfathomable plans.

What happens when soldiers are thrown into positions whence there is no escape? They will prefer death to flight, and facing death there is nothing they may not achieve; officers and men alike will put forth their uttermost strength.
How do soldiers act in desperate straits? They lose the sense of fear, stand firm if there is no refuge, show a stubborn front in hostile country, and fight hard if there is no help for it.
What do soldiers do without waiting to be marshaled, asked, restricted or ordered? They are on the qui vive, do your will, remain faithful, and can be trusted.
What happens when omens and superstitious doubts are prohibited? Until death itself comes, no calamity need be feared.

What did soldiers do on the day they were ordered out to battle, and what did they show when brought to bay? They wept, sitting up or lying down; but brought to bay they displayed the courage of a Chu or a Kuei.

To what may the skillful tactician be likened? To the shuai-jan, a snake of the Chung mountains: strike its head and the tail attacks; strike its tail and the head attacks; strike its middle and both head and tail attack.
Can an army imitate the shuai-jan? Yes; the men of Wu and Yueh are enemies, yet crossing a river in the same boat and caught by a storm, they assist each other as the left hand helps the right.
What is not enough in managing an army? It is not enough to trust in tethering horses and burying chariot wheels in the ground.
What is the principle of managing an army? Set up one standard of courage which all must reach.
What question involves the proper use of ground? How to make the best of both strong and weak.
How does a skillful general conduct his army? As though leading a single man, willy-nilly, by the hand.
What is the business of a general regarding secrecy and order? To be quiet and ensure secrecy, upright and just and maintain order.
How does a general mystify his officers and men? By false reports and appearances, keeping them in total ignorance.
How does a general keep the enemy without knowledge and prevent anticipation? By altering arrangements, changing plans, shifting camp, and taking circuitous routes.
What does a leader do at the critical moment? Like one who has climbed a height and kicks away the ladder, he carries his men deep into hostile territory before showing his hand.
What image describes a general driving his men? He burns his boats and breaks his cooking-pots; like a shepherd driving a flock, he drives them this way and that, and none knows whither he goes.
What may be termed the business of the general? To muster his host and bring it into danger.
What must most certainly be studied? The measures suited to the nine varieties of ground, the expediency of aggressive or defensive tactics, and the fundamental laws of human nature.
What is the general principle when invading hostile territory? Penetrating deeply brings cohesion; penetrating but a short way means dispersion.
What ground is reached on leaving one's own country and crossing neighborhood territory, and what ground has communication on all four sides? Critical ground, and ground of intersecting highways.
What ground is serious and what is facile? Deep penetration is serious ground; shallow penetration is facile ground.
What ground is hemmed-in and what is desperate? Enemy strongholds on the rear and narrow passes in front make hemmed-in ground; no place of refuge makes desperate ground.
What should be done on dispersive and facile ground? Inspire unity of purpose on dispersive ground, and see that all parts of the army are closely connected on facile ground.
What should be done on contentious ground? Hurry up the rear.
What should be done on open and intersecting-highway ground? Keep a vigilant eye on defenses on open ground, and consolidate alliances on intersecting highways.
What should be done on serious and difficult ground? Ensure a continuous stream of supplies on serious ground, and keep pushing along the road in difficult ground.
What should be done on hemmed-in and desperate ground? Block any way of retreat on hemmed-in ground, and proclaim the hopelessness of saving their lives on desperate ground.

What is the soldier's disposition when surrounded, helpless, or in danger? To offer obstinate resistance when surrounded, to fight hard when he cannot help himself, and to obey promptly when in danger.

What cannot be done until the designs of neighboring princes are known, until the country is familiar, and until local guides are used? Enter into alliances, lead an army on the march, and turn natural advantages to account.
What does not befit a warlike prince? To ignore any of the four or five principles of alliance, march, and natural advantage.
How does a warlike prince attacking a powerful state show generalship? By preventing the concentration of the enemy's forces, overawing opponents, and preventing allies from joining against him.

How does a warlike prince treat other states and his own designs? He does not strive to ally with all and sundry nor foster other states' power; he carries out his own secret designs, keeping antagonists in awe, and thus captures their cities and overthrows their kingdoms.
What happens when rewards are bestowed without regard to rule and orders issued without regard to previous arrangements? You can handle a whole army as though dealing with a single man.

What should soldiers be confronted with, and what should they be told? Confront them with the deed itself and never let them know your design; show them the bright outlook, but tell them nothing when the situation is gloomy.

What happens when an army is placed in deadly peril and desperate straits? It will survive and come off in safety; precisely when a force has fallen into harm's way it is capable of striking a blow for victory.
How is success in warfare gained? By carefully accommodating ourselves to the enemy's purpose.
What is achieved by persistently hanging on the enemy's flank? In the long run, killing the commander-in-chief; this is called ability to accomplish a thing by sheer cunning.
What should be done on the day one takes up command? Block the frontier passes, destroy the official tallies, and stop the passage of all emissaries.
How should one act in the council-chamber? Be stern, so that you may control the situation.
What should be done if the enemy leaves a door open? Rush in.
How should one forestall an opponent and time his arrival? Seize what he holds dear, and subtly contrive to time his arrival on the ground.
How should one walk and accommodate oneself to the enemy? Walk in the path defined by rule, and accommodate yourself to the enemy until you can fight a decisive battle.

How should one begin and end an engagement? Exhibit the coyness of a maiden until the enemy gives an opening; afterwards emulate the rapidity of a running hare, and it will be too late for the enemy to oppose you.
What does deep penetration into hostile territory produce, and what does shallow penetration produce? Deep penetration brings cohesion; shallow penetration means dispersion.
What ground lies beyond one's own country across neighborhood territory, and what ground has communication on all four sides? Critical ground, and intersecting highways.
What ground results from deep or shallow penetration into a country? Serious ground from deep penetration; facile ground from shallow penetration.
What ground results from enemy strongholds behind and narrow passes in front, or from no refuge at all? Hemmed-in ground, and desperate ground.
What is the effect of placing an army in deadly peril and desperate straits? It survives and comes off in safety; a force in harm's way can strike a blow for victory.

How is success in warfare gained, and what does hanging on the enemy's flank achieve? By accommodating ourselves to the enemy's purpose; hanging on his flank kills the commander-in-chief by sheer cunning.

What should be done on taking up command, and how should one act in the council-chamber? Block frontier passes, destroy tallies, stop emissaries, and be stern in the council-chamber to control the situation.
